summary: Describes extensions to OSPF for QoS routing, with focus on the algorithms for computing QoS routes and the information carried to support them. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A map-sharing method that picks roads by quality, like a smooth quick one, not just the shortest.

subtitle: Making routers choose paths based on quality, not just distance.

tldr.problem: OSPF finds the shortest path to send packets, but some applications need paths with specific quality: enough bandwidth, low delay, or both.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2676 extends OSPF to advertise available bandwidth and delay on each link, and adds a path selection algorithm that picks the path with the fewest hops that also has enough bandwidth, choosing the one with the most bandwidth available when multiple paths exist.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Experimental and was never standardized. Later work on QoS routing took different approaches. The core idea of advertising link metrics and computing paths remains relevant in modern networking.

today: RFC 2676 remains Experimental and was never standardized as an internet-wide approach to QoS routing. OSPF continues to be a hop-by-hop shortest-path protocol. QoS routing concepts have evolved in different directions: Differentiated Services (DiffServ) focuses on per-hop treatment rather than path selection, while newer approaches use segment routing or centralized software-defined networking (SDN) for QoS-aware routing.

sections.title: Why QoS Routing Matters
sections.content:
The Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) protocol tells routers how to send packets by computing the shortest path to each destination. However, "shortest" means the fewest hops, not the highest quality. Some applications, such as video calls or financial transactions, need not just any path but one that guarantees a certain amount of bandwidth or low delay.

Quality of Service (QoS) routing selects paths based on these quality metrics. An application might say "I need a path with at least 10 Mbps of bandwidth" or "the delay must be under 50 milliseconds." The routing protocol must know which paths can meet these requirements and pick the best one. RFC 2676 describes how to extend OSPF to support this.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a delivery service that sends packages via the quickest route. But what if some customers need their packages to arrive by tomorrow, not just as fast as possible? The service should check which routes are fast enough to meet the deadline, then pick the cheapest one.

sections.title: QoS Metrics and Path Selection
sections.content:
RFC 2676 identifies three key metrics for QoS routing. Available bandwidth is the amount of unused capacity on a link, which changes as traffic flows are added or removed. Propagation delay is the time it takes a signal to travel the physical link (important for links like satellite), which changes rarely. Hop count measures how many routers a path passes through, and the algorithm prefers paths with fewer hops.

The path selection algorithm uses a modified shortest-path algorithm called Bellman-Ford. It pre-computes paths to all destinations for all possible bandwidths. The result is a QoS routing table that answers questions like: "What is the maximum bandwidth available on a 3-hop path to network 10.0.0.0?" For any bandwidth requirement, the algorithm finds the path with the minimum number of hops that satisfies it, and when multiple such paths exist, it picks the one with the most bandwidth available (to leave room for other flows).
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm is like a navigator asking: "Which roads are clear enough for a truck that needs a 10-foot-wide lane? Among those roads, which has the fewest turns to the destination? If there are ties, which has the most extra space for other trucks?"

sections.title: OSPF Protocol Extensions
sections.content:
To support QoS, routers must advertise the available bandwidth and delay on each link using OSPF's Link State Advertisement (LSA) messages. RFC 2676 proposes using OSPF's Type of Service (TOS) field to encode QoS metrics, adding new "extended TOS" entries to LSAs. A router signals QoS support by setting a Q-bit in the options field of the LSA header.

Bandwidth is encoded in a 16-bit field using an exponential notation: a 3-bit exponent (base 8) followed by a 13-bit mantissa. This allows representing bandwidths from 8 bytes per second to over 17 terabits per second. Delay is encoded similarly, using base 4. The encoding is inverted (higher numeric value means lower available bandwidth) to ensure that misconfigured routers do not misinterpret bandwidth as a routing cost.

A critical question is when to send updates: if bandwidth is sent on every change, the network is flooded with updates; if updates are infrequent, routes may be computed with stale information. RFC 2676 discusses triggering updates when a metric crosses a threshold (absolute or percentage change), with optional hold-down timers to limit update frequency.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers gossip to each other about road conditions: how much lane space is available (bandwidth) and how long the drive takes (delay). They use a special code to pack this information into OSPF messages without breaking older routers that do not understand the code.

sections.title: Computing and Using QoS Routes
sections.content:
The RFC discusses two approaches for path computation. On-demand computation runs the path selection algorithm when a new flow arrives (e.g., when an RSVP request comes in). Pre-computation runs the algorithm periodically or after a fixed number of metric updates, building the QoS routing table in advance. Pre-computation amortizes the cost over many requests, but uses more computation per run (computing paths to all destinations for all bandwidths rather than for one destination and one bandwidth).

Once a path is selected for a flow, the RFC recommends keeping it stable and only recomputing when absolutely necessary (the flow stops or the selected path becomes inadequate). This requires tracking path "pinning" state and coordinating with signaling protocols like RSVP. The details of path management are outside the main focus of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: When a user requests a QoS route, the router either computes one right away (on-demand) or looks it up in a pre-computed table. Once a route is chosen, the router sticks with it and does not switch unless something goes wrong.

sections.title: Implementation and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 2676 includes a reference implementation in the GateD routing daemon (a Unix-based platform for implementing routing protocols). The implementation supports hop-by-hop routing (each router independently picks the next hop) but not explicit routing (where the source specifies the entire path). It assumes all routers in an area support QoS extensions and does not handle mixed environments with QoS-aware and non-QoS-aware routers.

The RFC identifies several open issues left for future work: support for multi-area routing with metric aggregation, External AS links, virtual links, and incremental updates. These limitations, combined with the Experimental status, mean the RFC was never adopted as a standard for internet-wide QoS routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors built a working version on a Unix computer to test the idea. But they left some hard problems unsolved, like how to handle very large networks with many routing areas.
